title: A spatial regression approach to modeling urban land surface temperature
author: Ismaila, Muhammed, et al.

steps.title: Select and Prepare Data
steps.instruction: Acquire Landsat and SRTM DEM data at 30 m spatial resolution for the study area (greater than 8000 hectares).

steps.title: Initialize Software Environment
steps.instruction: Set up the necessary GUI software packages for data processing and analysis.

steps.title: Calculate Spectral Indices
steps.instruction: Convert all relevant bands to top of atmosphere (ToA) reflectance and calculate the following indices using the specified bands:

substeps.instruction: Calculate NDBI using the formula: (SWIR1 - NIR) / (SWIR1 + NIR)
Calculate NDVI using the formula: (NIR - RED) / (NIR + RED)
Calculate MNDWI using the formula: (GREEN - SWIR1) / (GREEN + SWIR1)

steps.title: Retrieve Surface Albedo
steps.instruction: Retrieve Albedo from Landsat 8 OLI data based on Landsat 7 ETM+ equivalent using the following formula: Albedo = (0.356α2 + 0.130α4 + 0.373α5 + 0.085α6 + 0.072α7 - 0.0018) / (0.356 + 0.130 + 0.373 + 0.085 + 0.072), where α represents Landsat 8 OLI bands 2, 4, 5, 6, and 7.

steps.title: Perform Spatial Regression Modeling
steps.instruction: Construct a regression model to quantitatively measure the relationship between the dependent variable and independent variables.

substeps.instruction: Set Land Surface Temperature (LST) as the dependent variable
Set NDBI, NDVI, MNDWI, Albedo, and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) from SRTM data as the explanatory (independent) variables

description: Physical environment and geophysical features are investigated in order to better understand our environment and harness its resources. These studies are done using in situ-based measurements using probes. However, there are drawbacks due to inability of probes to sample large areas and be able to have repeated measurements over time. These limitations are handled by satellite measurements. Satellites are being developed to assist us in mapping our environment spatially over large areas using short time repeat cycles. The Landsat satellite series is useful for environmental research. Landsat data is used in a variety of applications around the world, including agriculture, forestry, and range resource management, land use and mapping, geology, hydrology, and coastal resources. Imagery with a moderate spatial resolution and multispectral capability is well suited to a wide range of applications ranging from modeling of population dynamics of disease vectors in association with habitat features to support for emergency response, environmental comfort, disaster relief and predictions [8]. Other areas include vector-borne diseases mapping such as malaria and dengue fever locations. These are compared to terrain data to study areas that are particularly conducive to their breeding in terms of height and moisture. These, along with rainfall, can be incorporated into vector capability models (VCAP) to simulate disease endemism [6]. Processing these data require prior knowledge of how satellite sensors work as well as understanding of atmospheric attenuation that occurs as sensor signals pass through the atmosphere. However, with the exception of a few issues such as cloud and haze, which are managed by atmospheric correction by end users, the majority of pre-processing work is performed by data providers prior to the release of data to the public.
